en: To make something impure or weaker by adding a cheaper or harmful substance
hook: ADULTERATE: an ADULT trick to cheat by mixing in cheap stuff.
story: Adulterate. To make something impure by mixing in something cheaper or harmful. Shelby's mother had bought turmeric powder from the same market stall for years. One day, a mobile court tested the stall's stock and found brick dust mixed into the bright yellow powder. Shelby's mother [gasp] stared at her jar. The seller had been adulterating it all along. Adulterate comes from a Latin verb meaning to corrupt: an adulterated product has been corrupted by cheap additions. So, what verb means to spoil something pure by mixing in an inferior substance? ... Adulterate.

gre.s: Inspectors discovered that the supplier had found a way to ____ the saffron with dyed corn silk, passing off the cheap filler as the costly spice.
gre.clue: passing off the cheap filler as the costly spice

example: Food inspectors in Dhaka fined several shops for adulterating turmeric powder with brick dust to increase its weight.

en: To increase the power, wealth, or importance of; to make something seem greater than it is
bn: ক্ষমতা বা মর্যাদা বাড়ানো; বাড়িয়ে দেখানো
hook: AG-GRAND-ize: to make yourself GRAND.
story: Aggrandize. To increase someone's power or importance, or to make something seem greater than it is. When a local businessman paid for a short new road, he had his name painted on six giant billboards along it. He told reporters the road would change the whole district. The villagers noticed it was barely half a kilometre long. He had used the road to aggrandize himself. Hear grand inside aggrandize: to aggrandize is to make someone or something look grander. So, what verb means to inflate one's own importance or power? ... Aggrandize.

gre.s: Rather than ____ his own role, the modest scientist repeatedly credited his students for the discovery.
gre.clue: the modest scientist repeatedly credited his students

example: The dictator's statues and portraits were designed to aggrandize a man who had never actually fought in a single battle.

en: To grow, spread, or multiply quickly
hook: BURGEON: a BURGER shop that grows into a giant chain overnight.
story: Burgeon. To grow or spread quickly. When Jasmine opened a tiny stall selling homemade rice cakes near her university gate, she had one stove and one helper. Within two years, her orders burgeoned. She now runs three shops, employs twelve women from her neighbourhood, and delivers to offices across the city. Her mother [laugh] still cannot believe it began with one frying pan. A burgeon was once a bud, and like buds bursting open in spring, a burgeoning business grows fast. So, what verb means to grow and flourish rapidly? ... Burgeon.

gre.s: Scientists warn that, unless strict controls are introduced, the city's population will continue to ____, straining already overloaded water supplies.
gre.clue: straining already overloaded water supplies

example: Online clothing shops have burgeoned across Bangladesh, with thousands of small sellers now taking orders through social media.

en: Cautious and wary; reluctant to give or risk
hook: CHARY: CAREFUL and wARY.
story: Chary. Cautious and wary; slow to give or to trust. Last year, Trevor lent his carefully written notes to a classmate, who copied them and passed them off as his own. Trevor's marks suffered. Now, when anyone asks for his notes, he hesitates, asks why, and shares only a page or two. He has become chary of lending anything. Chary comes from an old English word linked to care: a chary person takes great care before trusting. So, what word describes someone wary and reluctant to give or risk? ... Chary.

gre.s: Having lost heavily in the last market crash, investors were understandably ____ of new technology stocks, refusing to commit money without years of proven profits.
gre.clue: refusing to commit money without years of proven profits

example: After being cheated once by a fake recruiting agency, Kamal was chary of any job offer that asked for money in advance.

en: To restrict within limits; to draw a line around
hook: CIRCUM-SCRIBE: draw (scribe) a CIRCLE around it.
story: Circumscribe. To restrict something within limits; literally, to draw a line around it. Karen's grandmother was the best student in her village school in the nineteen sixties. But at fifteen she was married, and her world shrank to one kitchen, one courtyard and one household. She never stopped reading the newspaper, word by word, by the window. Her life had been circumscribed by others, yet her mind had not. Circum means around, as in circle, and scribe means write: to circumscribe is to draw a boundary around. So, what verb means to confine something within narrow limits? ... Circumscribe.

gre.s: The new law sought to ____ the president's powers, limiting his ability to declare emergencies without parliamentary approval.
gre.clue: limiting his ability to declare emergencies

example: Her illness circumscribed her travels, but from her balcony in Old Dhaka she wrote vivid stories about the whole country.

en: An unexpected, embarrassing mishap or minor dispute
hook: CONTRE-TEMPS: French for 'against time' — bad timing.
story: Contretemps. An awkward, unexpected mishap or a small quarrel. At Jody's engagement, the groom's aunt arrived wearing exactly the same red silk sari as Jody's mother. The two women stopped at the gate and looked each other up and down, and the guests [gasp] went silent. Then Jody's mother [laugh] took the aunt's arm and insisted they pose for a photo together. The little contretemps became everyone's favourite story of the night. Contretemps is French for against the time: a moment that goes wrong at the worst possible time. So, what noun means an embarrassing little mishap or squabble? ... Contretemps.

gre.s: The diplomats' brief ____ over seating arrangements, though embarrassing at the time, was soon forgotten amid the far weightier negotiations that followed.
gre.clue: soon forgotten amid the far weightier negotiations

example: A minor contretemps over who would cut the wedding cake briefly soured the mood between the two families.

en: To capture someone's complete attention; to fascinate
hook: ENTHRALL: like a THRALL (slave) to the story.
story: Enthrall. To hold someone's complete attention; to fascinate. During a long power cut in a quiet village, the children gathered around Mark's grandfather on the dark veranda. He told them about a giant fish that lived under the old bridge, his voice dropping low, a lantern flickering on his face. Nobody moved. Nobody even swatted the mosquitoes. The story enthralled them. A thrall was a slave in old English, so an enthralling story holds you as its captive. So, what verb means to capture someone's full attention? ... Enthrall.

gre.s: Her storytelling could ____ even the most restless audience: children who usually fidgeted through lessons sat motionless until the final word.
gre.clue: children who usually fidgeted through lessons sat motionless until the final word

example: The documentary on deep-sea creatures enthralled my younger brother, who watched it four times in a single weekend.

en: To give unclear answers on purpose so as not to take a stand
hook: EQUI-VOCATE: EQUAL VOICES, saying both yes and no at once.
story: Equivocate. To give vague answers on purpose, so as not to commit to anything. When Faye asked her landlord directly whether the rent would rise next year, he smiled. "Well, it depends. Prices change. We will see. Maybe yes, maybe not, it is hard to say." She asked again and got another cloud of words. [sigh] He was equivocating. Equi means equal and voc means voice: someone who equivocates speaks with two equal voices, yes and no at once. So, what verb means to dodge a question with deliberately unclear answers? ... Equivocate.

gre.s: Pressed to say whether she supported the bill, the candidate continued to ____, offering answers so qualified that both sides claimed her as an ally.
gre.clue: offering answers so qualified that both sides claimed her

example: When the journalist asked whether layoffs were planned, the company spokesman equivocated, saying only that all options were being studied.

en: To attack someone or something with fierce criticism
hook: EX-CORIATE: to strip off the skin (corium), with harsh words.
story: Excoriate. To criticise someone extremely harshly. Six months after a new bridge opened over a coastal canal, a long crack split its deck. Engineers found that the builders had used far less steel than the plan required. In parliament and in every newspaper, the contractors were excoriated. One editorial called the bridge a monument to greed. Excoriate comes from the Latin for stripping off the skin, so to excoriate someone is to flay them with words. So, what verb means to criticise with fierce severity? ... Excoriate.

gre.s: Reviewers did not merely criticize the novel; they chose to ____ it, condemning its plot, its prose, and its author's integrity in the harshest possible terms.
gre.clue: in the harshest possible terms

example: In a fiery editorial, the newspaper excoriated the factory owners who had locked the fire exits.

en: To show or declare that someone is not guilty
hook: EX-CULPA: out of (ex) guilt (culpa, culprit).
story: Exculpate. To show or declare that someone is not guilty. When a gold bangle disappeared from a city house, the family blamed their young housekeeper, Shirley. She wept and swore she had not taken it. A week later, a plumber clearing the bathroom drain pulled out the missing bangle, slipped from the owner's own wrist. The discovery exculpated Shirley completely, and the family begged her forgiveness. Ex means out of, and culpa means guilt, as in culprit: to exculpate is to lift someone out of guilt. So, what verb means to clear someone of blame? ... Exculpate.

gre.s: The newly discovered letters seemed to ____ the accused general, showing that he had opposed the massacre rather than ordered it.
gre.clue: showing that he had opposed the massacre rather than ordered it

example: DNA tests finally exculpated the farmer, who had spent eleven years in prison for a murder he did not commit.

en: Inclined to cause disagreement and division into factions
hook: FACTIOUS: creating FACTIONS.
story: Factious. Causing disagreement and splitting a group into rival sides. The drama club at Shannon's college had always felt like a family. Then two senior members began fighting over who would direct the spring play. Soon every rehearsal split into two camps that sat on opposite sides of the room and refused to share props. The play was cancelled. Their factious quarrel had broken the club. Factious comes from faction, a rival group within a group: a factious person creates factions. So, what word describes behaviour that splits a group into warring sides? ... Factious.

gre.s: The once unified party had grown so ____ that its members spent more energy attacking rival wings than opposing the government.
gre.clue: spent more energy attacking rival wings than opposing the government

example: The factious student union split into three groups that could not agree even on the date of the annual festival.

en: To deny or contradict
hook: GAINSAY: to say AGAINST.
story: Gainsay. To deny or contradict something. At the cricket club meeting, a senior member insisted that the young spinner, Ryder, was not good enough for the first team. Then the coach simply read out the season's figures: the most wickets, the best economy, and two match-winning spells in the final week. Nobody could gainsay those numbers. [chuckle] The senior member quietly sat down. Gain here is an old form of against, so to gainsay is to say against. So, what verb means to deny or contradict something? ... Gainsay.

gre.s: No one could ____ the champion's skill; even her fiercest critics admitted that she was the finest player of her generation.
gre.clue: even her fiercest critics admitted

example: There is no gainsaying the importance of the garment sector, which employs millions of workers across Bangladesh.

en: Not fitting the rules of polite, proper behavior
hook: IN-DECOROUS: NOT showing DECORUM.
story: Indecorous. Not in keeping with good manners or proper behaviour. During the quiet moment of a wedding ceremony, just as the officiant asked the bride for her consent, a guest's phone rang loudly with a film song. Instead of silencing it, he answered and began discussing cricket scores at full volume. Elders turned and frowned. Lina's grandmother shook her head at such indecorous behaviour. Indecorous is the opposite of decorous, from decorum, the rules of proper conduct. So, what word describes behaviour that is improper for the occasion? ... Indecorous.

gre.s: Many guests found the best man's crude jokes at the memorial service ____, since such levity seemed out of place at so solemn an occasion.
gre.clue: seemed out of place at so solemn an occasion

example: Several members of parliament considered it indecorous for a minister to dance on stage at a campaign rally.

en: Unable to be avoided; inevitable
hook: IN-E-LUCTABLE: you can't struggle (luctari) out of it.
story: Ineluctable. Impossible to avoid; certain to happen. All winter, Sam found reasons to skip his exam preparation: a wedding, a cricket series, a cold. He hoped for a strike, a flood, anything that might postpone the board exam. But the date did not move. On the morning itself, he sat in the hall with a pen in his trembling hand. The exam had been ineluctable all along. Ineluctable comes from the Latin for something you cannot struggle out of: no matter how you wriggle, it arrives. So, what word describes something you simply cannot escape? ... Ineluctable.

gre.s: Many historians once believed the empire's decline was ____, the result of forces no ruler could have resisted; newer scholarship stresses specific mistakes that might easily have been avoided.
gre.clue: forces no ruler could have resisted

example: Rising sea levels make the ineluctable retreat of some coastal villages a matter of planning rather than debate.

en: To persuade someone by flattery or deception
hook: INVEIGLE: like a VEIL over the truth to lure someone in.
story: Inveigle. To persuade someone by flattery or trickery into doing something. A smooth-talking agent visited Ryan's grandfather. He praised the old man's wisdom, drank tea with him three afternoons in a row, and spoke of a scheme that would double his savings in a year. At last the grandfather handed over his pension savings. Only later did the family discover the scheme was a fraud. He had been inveigled. Inveigle comes from a French word meaning to blind: an inveigler blinds you with sweet talk. So, what verb means to lure someone into something through deception? ... Inveigle.

gre.s: Through a combination of flattery and false promises, the con artist managed to ____ several elderly investors into handing over their life savings.
gre.clue: Through a combination of flattery and false promises

example: With flattering letters and fake awards, a bogus publisher inveigled dozens of first-time poets in Khulna into paying for worthless print runs.

en: To scold or criticize someone fiercely
hook: LAMBASTE: LAMB gets BASTED (beaten) with harsh words.
story: Lambaste. To criticise or scold someone fiercely. Nick's team handed in a project report full of copied paragraphs and careless errors. The next morning, their professor held it up before the whole class and lambasted them for twenty minutes: lazy research, sloppy writing, no respect for the reader. Nick's ears burned. He rewrote every page that week. Lambaste joins two old English verbs, lam and baste, both meaning to beat: to lambaste is to give someone a verbal beating. So, what verb means to scold someone fiercely? ... Lambaste.

gre.s: Rather than praising the minister's long-delayed reforms, opposition leaders chose to ____ them as too little, too late, and a betrayal of earlier promises.
gre.clue: too little, too late, and a betrayal of earlier promises

example: Food bloggers lambasted the new restaurant on Gulshan Avenue for serving cold biryani at outrageous prices.

en: A heavy tiredness that drains body or mind of energy
hook: LASSITUDE: a LAZY attitude.
story: Lassitude. A heavy tiredness that drains body and mind of energy. During an April heatwave in the north, the temperature stayed above forty degrees for a week. Bella could barely lift her books. The ceiling fan only pushed hot air around, the streets were empty by noon, and even the stray dogs lay flat in the shade. A deep lassitude settled over the whole city. Lassitude comes from the Latin lassus, meaning weary; do not confuse it with latitude, which is about freedom or distance. So, what noun means a heavy, draining weariness? ... Lassitude.

gre.s: The sweltering afternoon induced a general ____ among the delegates; several dozed in their seats, and no one had the energy to challenge the chairman's proposals.
gre.clue: no one had the energy to challenge the chairman's proposals

example: Weeks of dengue fever left Rumana in a lassitude so deep that she could barely climb the stairs to her flat.

en: To make a great public fuss over someone
bn: বীরের মতো সম্মান করা; তারকা বানিয়ে দেওয়া
hook: LIONIZE: treated like the LION, king of the jungle.
story: Lionize. To treat someone as a celebrity and make a great public fuss over them. When a fisherman's daughter from a coastal island won a gold medal at an international mathematics contest, she flew home to a crowd at the airport. Television channels interviewed her, and her school named a classroom after her. She was lionized everywhere she went, [laugh] though mostly she wanted to sleep. To lionize someone is to treat them like a lion, the most admired animal of all. So, what verb means to treat someone as a celebrity? ... Lionize.

gre.s: Although the press rushed to ____ the scientist after her discovery, she found the constant attention exhausting and retreated from public life.
gre.clue: she found the constant attention exhausting

example: When the young mountaineer returned from Everest, newspapers lionized her and schools invited her to speak every week.

en: Noisy and difficult to control
hook: OBSTREPEROUS: makes an OBSTACLE with noise.
story: Obstreperous. Noisy and hard to control. The night train to the coast was quiet until a group of young men boarded at a junction. They played music on loudspeakers, shouted across the carriage, and argued with the ticket checker who asked them to sit down. Children woke and cried. When the guard finally moved the obstreperous group to the last coach, the passengers breathed with relief. Obstreperous comes from a Latin verb meaning to roar against: an obstreperous crowd roars against all control. So, what word describes people who are noisy and unruly? ... Obstreperous.

gre.s: The substitute teacher could not control the ____ students, who shouted over one another, ignored her instructions, and refused to stay in their seats.
gre.clue: shouted over one another, ignored her instructions

example: The flight attendants had to calm an obstreperous passenger who kept shouting about the delay and pounding the seat.

en: Transparently clear; easily understood
hook: PELLUCID: like LUCID, light shines through.
story: Pellucid. Perfectly clear; easy to understand. In her first statistics class, Tamara was terrified of probability. Then Professor Hayes walked in with a jar of red and white marbles. He drew them out one at a time, wrote each result on the board, and built the whole idea slowly from what everyone could see. By the end of the hour, Tamara [gasp] understood it completely. His explanation was pellucid. Pellucid contains lucid, from the Latin for light: a pellucid explanation lets the light shine right through. So, what word describes an explanation so clear that anyone can follow it? ... Pellucid.

gre.s: The textbook's ____ explanations, free of jargon and full of simple examples, made a notoriously difficult subject accessible to beginners.
gre.clue: free of jargon and full of simple examples

example: The physicist's pellucid lecture on black holes left even the history students in the audience nodding along.

en: Quick to notice and understand what others miss
hook: PERSPICACIOUS: PERCEPTIVE, sees through everything.
story: Perspicacious. Quick to notice and understand what others miss. Everyone at a small export company admired the polite new accountant. Only Sheila, the oldest clerk, noticed that his invoices always ended in round numbers and that he never took a holiday. She checked quietly and uncovered a scheme that had been draining money for a year. Her boss called her the most perspicacious person in the building. Perspicacious comes from a Latin verb meaning to see through: a perspicacious mind sees through appearances. So, what word describes someone sharp enough to notice what everyone else misses? ... Perspicacious.

gre.s: A ____ observer of political trends, she foresaw the government's collapse months before other analysts noticed even the first signs of trouble.
gre.clue: foresaw the government's collapse months before other analysts

example: A perspicacious bank teller noticed that the signature on the cheque was slightly off and quietly called the manager.

en: To be an early sign or representation of something later
hook: PRE-FIGURE: a FIGURE of what's coming BEFORE it arrives.
story: Prefigure. To be an early sign or picture of something that comes later. At eight, Tess took apart the family radio and rebuilt it, with one screw left over. [laugh] Her grandfather saw something more. Twenty years later, Tess was leading a team that builds small satellites. That afternoon with the radio had prefigured her whole career. Pre means before, and a figure is a shape: to prefigure is to show the shape of something before it arrives. So, what verb means to be an early hint of what is to come? ... Prefigure.

gre.s: The architect's student sketches, with their sweeping curves and conspicuous absence of right angles, seem to ____ the radical designs that would later make her famous.
gre.clue: that would later make her famous

example: The young cricketer's fearless innings in school matches prefigured the attacking style that later made him a national star.

en: To speak or act evasively to avoid the truth
bn: সত্য এড়িয়ে যাওয়া; ঘুরিয়ে কথা বলা
hook: PREVARICATE: PRE-VARY the truth, twist it.
story: Prevaricate. To speak evasively in order to avoid telling the truth. Ryan's mother asked him directly whether he had gone to his coaching class that afternoon. "Well, I was near the coaching centre," he said, "and I saw some friends, and the traffic was terrible, and the teacher often starts late anyway." She folded her arms. [chuckle] He was prevaricating, and they both knew it. Prevaricate comes from a Latin verb meaning to walk crookedly: a prevaricator walks around the truth instead of straight to it. So, what verb means to dodge the truth with evasive talk? ... Prevaricate.

gre.s: Pressed repeatedly about the missing funds, the treasurer continued to ____, offering vague answers that neither admitted nor denied any wrongdoing.
gre.clue: offering vague answers that neither admitted nor denied any wrongdoing

example: Asked by her mother where she had spent the afternoon, Tania prevaricated, mumbling something about a group study session.

en: Using too many words; tediously lengthy
hook: PROLIX: PRO at being LONG.
story: Prolix. Using far too many words; tediously long. At a wedding reception, the bride's uncle was asked to say a few words of blessing. He spoke for forty minutes. He began with his own childhood, quoted three poets and repeated every point twice, while the biryani grew cold on the tables. Nobody remembered a word of that prolix speech. Prolix comes from a Latin word meaning stretched out: a prolix speech stretches on far past its point. So, what word describes speech or writing that is wordy and tedious? ... Prolix.

gre.s: The editor urged the author to cut the manuscript in half, complaining that its ____ style buried every interesting idea under pages of needless detail.
gre.clue: buried every interesting idea under pages of needless detail

example: The ministry's prolix report ran to nine hundred pages, but its real findings could have fit on a single sheet.

en: To win or regain someone's favor by pleasing them
bn: তুষ্ট করা; সন্তুষ্ট করে প্রসন্ন করা
hook: PROPITIATE: make them PROPITIOUS (favorable) again.
story: Propitiate. To win or regain someone's favour by doing something to please them. Shawn forgot his wife's birthday. The next morning he came home from the bazaar with a big fish, a bunch of white tuberose flowers and a box of her favourite sweets. Then he cooked the fish himself, [chuckle] rather badly. She tried to stay angry but finally laughed. He had propitiated her. Propitiate is related to propitious, meaning favourable: to propitiate someone is to make them favourable to you again. So, what verb means to soothe someone's anger and win back their favour? ... Propitiate.

gre.s: Hoping to ____ the furious shareholders, the board announced a generous special dividend and promised to replace the chief executive whose blunders had cost them so much.
gre.clue: announced a generous special dividend

example: To propitiate his angry wife after forgetting their anniversary, Habib cooked her favorite hilsa curry and bought jasmine garlands.

en: Complaining in a whining or irritable way
hook: QUERULOUS: always QUERYING and complaining.
story: Querulous. Complaining in a whining, irritable way. Mister Chandler on the third floor complains about everything. The lift is too slow, the guard sleeps too much, the children downstairs are too loud, the mango seller cheats him, and even the rain falls at the wrong time. Each complaint comes in the same thin, peevish voice, and the building manager hides when he sees him coming. Mister Chandler is querulous. Querulous comes from a Latin verb meaning to complain, the same root that gives us quarrel. So, what word describes someone who constantly complains in a whiny voice? ... Querulous.

gre.s: Age had made the once-genial professor ____: he now found fault with every seminar, every meal, and every student, and his letters to the dean consisted largely of complaints.
gre.clue: his letters to the dean consisted largely of complaints

example: The querulous passenger in the next seat complained about the food, the temperature and the movie throughout the long flight.

en: Known only to a few experts; hard to grasp
hook: RECONDITE: RE-CON-DITE, hidden like a secret condo deep in the hills.
story: Recondite. Known only to a few experts; obscure and hard to understand. At a university seminar, a visiting scholar spoke for two hours on the grammar of an ancient Buddhist text, in a language few people still read. Sami understood perhaps one sentence in ten. Yet the five specialists in the front row nodded eagerly, taking notes. The subject was recondite. Recondite comes from a Latin word meaning hidden away: recondite knowledge is tucked away where few can reach it. So, what word describes knowledge known only to a small circle of experts? ... Recondite.

gre.s: Although the treatise addresses ____ questions of medieval theology, its author writes so clearly that even general readers can follow it.
gre.clue: even general readers can follow it

example: The old librarian could answer recondite questions about Mughal coinage that stumped even university professors.

en: Sleepy; drowsy; causing sleep
hook: SOMNOLENT: like inSOMNIA's opposite; full of sleep.
story: Somnolent. Sleepy and drowsy; also, causing sleep. After a holiday lunch of spiced rice, creamy beef curry, chicken roast and three kinds of dessert, Sid's whole family drifted to the living room. The ceiling fan hummed, the curtains glowed in the afternoon light, and his grandfather's soft snoring set a slow rhythm. One by one, every cousin fell asleep on the floor. It was a somnolent afternoon. Somnolent comes from the Latin somnus, meaning sleep, the same root as insomnia. So, what word describes a drowsy, sleepy mood? ... Somnolent.

gre.s: The ____ atmosphere of the warm lecture hall, combined with the speaker's monotone, left half the audience struggling to stay awake.
gre.clue: left half the audience struggling to stay awake

example: On a hot afternoon the somnolent village seemed deserted, with only a few goats wandering past the closed shops.

en: To plead for something humbly and earnestly
hook: SUPPLICATE: on your knees, SUPPLYING prayers.
story: Supplicate. To plead humbly and earnestly for something. When the great river swallowed his family's land, an old farmer named Joe travelled to the district office. He waited on a bench all day. When the officer finally called him in, Joe folded his hands and begged for a small plot on the new embankment, enough for a house and a few chickens. He supplicated without pride, for his grandchildren. Supplicate comes from a Latin verb meaning to bend down and plead: a supplicant bends low and begs. So, what verb means to beg humbly and earnestly? ... Supplicate.

gre.s: Defeated and desperate, the rebel leaders could only ____ the emperor, kneeling humbly before the very throne they had once vowed to destroy.
gre.clue: kneeling humbly before the very throne

example: Standing before the visa officer, the elderly man could only supplicate for permission to attend his son's graduation abroad.

en: To weaken or ruin something so it no longer works properly
hook: VITIATE: makes it VICIOUS, corrupts it.
story: Vitiate. To spoil or weaken something so that it no longer works properly. For six months, Isabel's team grew rice seedlings in a university greenhouse to test a new fertiliser. Then they discovered that a helper had been watering the untreated trays from the wrong tank, one already mixed with fertiliser. [gasp] That one mistake vitiated the entire experiment, and the data could not be trusted. Vitiate comes from the Latin vitium, meaning fault or vice: a single fault can vitiate a whole result. So, what verb means to spoil something by introducing a flaw? ... Vitiate.

gre.s: A single undisclosed conflict of interest can ____ an otherwise rigorous study, rendering its conclusions suspect.
gre.clue: rendering its conclusions suspect

example: A missing signature on the final page vitiated the entire land contract, and the sale had to begin again.
